  "text": "The laundrette had one rule taped above the machines: CHECK EVERY POCKET BEFORE WASHING.

I found a tooth in my husband's trousers.

Not a child's tooth. A molar, its roots still pink.

Martin had been dead for six weeks. These were the clothes the hospital had returned.

I wrapped it in a receipt and loaded the machine.

Halfway through the cycle, something tapped against the glass.

A wedding ring.

I checked my necklace. His ring was still there, hanging beside mine.

Inside the drum, the second ring turned slowly on a finger.

I pressed STOP.

The attendant looked up from her crossword.

“Don't do that.”

“There's something in there.”

“Usually is.”

A palm flattened against the window. I knew the scar beneath its thumb. Martin had cut himself opening oysters on our honeymoon.

The attendant came over and pressed START.

“He won't be right unless you finish.”

I watched a shoulder rise among the wet clothes. Then his face appeared, eyes closed, cheek pressed to the glass.

“What happens when it finishes?”

She glanced at the receipt in my hand.

“You checked the pockets?”

I unwrapped the tooth.

For the first time, she looked frightened.

The machine chimed.

Behind the glass, Martin opened his eyes. He smiled, showing a dark gap at the back of his mouth.

“Put it in,” the attendant whispered.

The door clicked open.

My husband unfolded onto the tiles, coughing warm, soapy water. I reached for him.

He caught my wrist and examined the tooth.

“That's not mine,” he said.

From the machine behind us came three polite knocks."
